newsitem.title: USA: Hubble service call tricky for U.S. astronauts.
newsitem.headline: Hubble service call tricky for U.S. astronauts.

text.p: A fragile set of solar panels will make NASA's second service call to the $2 billion Hubble Space Telescope a tricky task, but astronomers say the scientific rewards are worth the risk.
The space shuttle Discovery, with seven astronauts aboard, is scheduled to blastoff at 3:56 a.m. EST (0856 GMT) on Tuesday and rendezvous with the orbiting observatory two days later.
During the 10-day mission, four spacewalks are planned to install new scientific instruments aboard the telescope and upgrade some of the observatory's ageing components.

When NASA astronauts first visited the telescope in 1993, they successful repaired its blurred vision and helped restore the space agency's tarnished reputation. Now the telescope is working well and the Hubble's new service crew is feeling a different kind of pressure.
"Last time they really needed to succeed, but the telescope had not been producing great science prior to that," said Gregory Harbaugh, one of the mission's four spacewalking astronauts.
"Now the telescope is producing great science and we could go up there and screw it up," he said. "We sure don't want to do that. Our going in position is 'Above all else, do no harm.'"
The astronauts' work will be complicated by the telescope's delicate wing-like solar panels called arrays, which officials fear could buckle and fold up if disturbed.

The electricity-generating panels were installed by the last Hubble repair crew, but the harsh environment of space has left them fragile and twisted. Without electrical power the telescope would be rendered useless.

"The solar arrays are a big challenge," said flight director Jeff Bantle, who will orchestrate the service call from mission control in Houston. "There's some risk involved. We are not carrying any spares."

One of the arrays may be bent over as much as 20 inches (51 cm), he said. The arrays, which were built by the European Space Agency, are to be replaced with rigid solar panels during the next Hubble servicing mission scheduled for 1999.

Discovery's astronauts have trained to perform their tasks with a delicate touch and will avoid any direct contact with the arrays. They are also prepared to install specially designed "splints" to brace an array should it collapse.

"We would not like to do that unless we have to," Bantle said. "There's some risk in putting those (splints) in. Those arrays are awful sensitive and I think the least amount of disturbance we can put to them the better."
The margin for error is slim. During some tasks, the shuttle's robot arm will come as close as eight inches (20 cm) to the fragile arrays as it moves astronauts to their work sites on the telescope.
"We just have to get there and see what the situation is," Harbaugh said. "If the arrays are any worse than expected we're going to be very challenged."
The primary goal of the service call will be to install two new scientific instruments, both about the size of a telephone booth.
"The dramatic improvement in science that these instruments provide is well worth the risk involved in this mission," said Ed Weiller, chief scientist for the Hubble Space Telescope.

The first instrument, it's detectors chilled to minus 355 degrees Fahrenheit (-215C), will give Hubble its first view of the Universe in infrared light. The second will allow astronomers to detect the composition and velocity of distant objects in unprecedented detail. It will be particularly useful for the detection of black holes.
"We are replacing 1970s technology in our science instruments with 1990s technology," Weiller said.
